course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

topic.title: Election of 1860 and Secession
topic.summary: How the election of 1860 split the parties, why most slave states seceded after Lincoln's victory, and how the firing on Fort Sumter began the Civil War.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: In the presidential election of 1860, the Democratic Party
choices: united behind Stephen Douglas, who won most of the Southern states
split, with Northern and Southern wings nominating different candidates
nominated Abraham Lincoln on a platform to stop the spread of slavery
chose not to run a candidate and instead backed the Constitutional Union ticket
questions.explanation: Northern Democrats nominated Douglas and Southern Democrats nominated Breckinridge, which divided the party's vote.
choiceExplanations: The party split, and Douglas won few states.
Northern Democrats nominated Douglas and Southern Democrats nominated Breckinridge, which divided the party's vote.
Lincoln was the Republican nominee.
The Democrats ran two candidates.
questions.distinguisher: The united behind Douglas choice is close because Douglas was the leading Democrat, but Southern Democrats refused to support him.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Abraham Lincoln won the presidency in 1860
choices: with a majority of the popular vote but few electoral votes
with the support of most Southern states after promising to protect slavery
after the House of Representatives chose him when no one won a majority
with a majority of electoral votes but no electoral votes from the South
questions.explanation: Lincoln carried the free states, and a divided opposition gave him a majority of the electoral vote without Southern support.
choiceExplanations: He won about 40 percent of the popular vote.
He won no Southern electoral votes.
The Electoral College gave him a majority.
Lincoln carried the free states, and a divided opposition gave him a majority of the electoral vote without Southern support.
questions.distinguisher: The popular vote choice is close because Lincoln's victory was lawful, but he won about 40 percent of the popular vote and not a majority.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The decision of Southern states to secede after Lincoln's election is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: Fear that a Republican president would stop the spread of slavery and weaken Southern power
A demand by Lincoln that the Southern states end slavery immediately
A Republican plan to raise the tariff on cotton sold to Britain
A Supreme Court decision that had banned slavery in the Southern states
questions.explanation: Southern leaders feared that the new administration would stop the spread of slavery and would reduce the South's place in the Union.
choiceExplanations: Southern leaders feared that the new administration would stop the spread of slavery and would reduce the South's place in the Union.
Lincoln promised not to interfere with slavery in the states.
The Republicans had no such plan.
The Court had ruled in favor of slaveholders.
questions.distinguisher: The immediate end choice is close because Lincoln opposed slavery, but he pledged not to interfere with it in the states where it existed.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a cause of the secession of Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina?
choices: Lincoln's election in November 1860, which led them to secede with the first seven states
The passage of the Crittenden Compromise, which they believed betrayed the South
Lincoln's call for troops to put down the rebellion after the attack on Fort Sumter
The Confederate victory at Bull Run, which showed that the South would win the war
questions.explanation: Many in the Upper South opposed secession until the president asked them to send troops against other Southern states.
choiceExplanations: These four states waited until after Fort Sumter.
The Crittenden Compromise did not pass.
Many in the Upper South opposed secession until the president asked them to send troops against other Southern states.
Bull Run was fought in July 1861, after they had left.
questions.distinguisher: The election of Lincoln choice is close because it caused the first states to leave, but these four stayed until Lincoln called for troops.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following were the border states that kept slavery but stayed in the Union?
choices: Virginia, Tennessee, Arkansas, and North Carolina
Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri
Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, and Georgia
Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Iowa
questions.explanation: Four slave states stayed loyal, and Lincoln worked to keep them because of their location and resources.
choiceExplanations: Those four states joined the Confederacy.
Four slave states stayed loyal, and Lincoln worked to keep them because of their location and resources.
Those states belonged to the Deep South and seceded.
Those states had abolished slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The Virginia, Tennessee, Arkansas, and North Carolina choice is close because they were also slave states of the Upper South, but they seceded.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the views of Lincoln and Southern leaders in 1861 about the Union?
choices: Lincoln held that the Union was perpetual, and Southern leaders that states could leave it
Lincoln held that states could leave the Union, and Southern leaders that it was perpetual
Lincoln wanted slavery ended in the states, and Southern leaders wanted it to remain
Lincoln held that secession needed the consent of Congress, and Southern leaders that it needed a popular vote
questions.explanation: Lincoln argued that no state could lawfully leave the Union, and Southern leaders claimed a right to secede.
choiceExplanations: Lincoln argued that no state could lawfully leave the Union, and Southern leaders claimed a right to secede.
The views are reversed.
Lincoln pledged not to end slavery in the states.
Lincoln denied that any state could lawfully leave.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed choice is close because it names the same two views, but it gives each side the position of the other.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The Crittenden Compromise of 1860 is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The Compromise of 1850, which had admitted California as a free state
A plan to end slavery gradually in the border states with payment to owners
A treaty with Britain that had settled the boundary of the Oregon country
Efforts to keep the Union together by protecting slavery south of the line at 36°30′
questions.explanation: Senator Crittenden proposed amendments to protect slavery in the territories south of the line, in the hope of keeping the South in the Union.
choiceExplanations: That Compromise was passed ten years earlier.
Crittenden's plan protected slavery.
The Oregon treaty was signed in 1846.
Senator Crittenden proposed amendments to protect slavery in the territories south of the line, in the hope of keeping the South in the Union.
questions.distinguisher: The Compromise of 1850 choice is close because both plans sought to preserve the Union, but the Crittenden plan came as the Southern states were seceding.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Confederate States of America was formed in February 1861 by
choices: all fifteen slave states, with Robert E. Lee as its first president
Southern Democrats who remained in Congress, with Stephen Douglas as leader
seven Southern states that had left the Union, with Jefferson Davis as president
the states of the Upper South after the firing on Fort Sumter began the war
questions.explanation: South Carolina and six other states of the Deep South formed a new government and chose Davis as president.
choiceExplanations: Only seven states had left, and Davis was president.
The Confederacy was formed outside the Union.
South Carolina and six other states of the Deep South formed a new government and chose Davis as president.
The Confederacy was formed before Fort Sumter.
questions.distinguisher: The all fifteen slave states choice is close because the Confederacy later grew to eleven states, but it began with seven and had Davis as its president.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Lincoln most likely addressed “my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen” in order to
choices: ask Congress to declare war on the states that had left the Union
persuade Southerners that the choice between peace and civil war was theirs
announce an end to slavery in the states that had left the Union
assure Northern voters that the Republicans had given up their platform
questions.explanation: Lincoln says that “in your hands . . . is the momentous issue of civil war,” and that the government “will not assail you.”
choiceExplanations: The excerpt says the government will not assail them.
Lincoln says that “in your hands . . . is the momentous issue of civil war,” and that the government “will not assail you.”
He says that he has no purpose to interfere with slavery.
He speaks to Southerners and keeps his position.
questions.distinguisher: The declare war choice is close because the speech came as the Union broke apart, but Lincoln said that the Southerners would be the aggressors.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.7, KC-5.2.II.D: after a series of contested debates about secession, most slave states voted to secede from the Union
stimulusBlocks.attribution: President Abraham Lincoln, in his First Inaugural Address on March 4, 1861, after seven Southern states had declared that they had left the Union
stimulusBlocks.citation: Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address (March 4, 1861). NLTK inaugural corpus, 1861-Lincoln.txt.
stimulusBlocks.note: By “the institution of slavery in the States where it exists,” Lincoln means slavery in the Southern states, as opposed to slavery in the territories.
stimulusBlocks.text:
I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists. I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so.

I hold that in contemplation of universal law and of the Constitution the Union of these States is perpetual.

In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war. The Government will not assail you. You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors. You have no oath registered in heaven to destroy the Government, while I shall have the most solemn one to “preserve, protect, and defend it.”

questions.subskillText: Identify a source’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims about slavery is best supported by the first paragraph of the excerpt?
choices: Lincoln promised to end slavery in the states by an act of Congress
Lincoln promised to ban slavery from the territories that were still unsettled
Lincoln promised that slavery could spread to the western territories
Lincoln promised not to interfere with slavery in the states where it existed
questions.explanation: Lincoln says, “I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists.”
choiceExplanations: He says that he has no lawful right to do so.
The paragraph concerns slavery in the states.
He opposed the spread of slavery.
Lincoln says, “I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists.”
questions.distinguisher: The territories choice is close because the Republican platform did oppose the spread of slavery, but the paragraph speaks only of slavery in the states.

questions.prompt: Lincoln's statement that “the Union of these States is perpetual” is best understood as a response to
choices: the claim of Southern leaders that states could leave the Union
the claim of some abolitionists that the free states should leave the Union
a proposal from Britain that the states form a looser confederation
the ruling in Dred Scott that Congress could not govern the territories
questions.explanation: Seven states had already seceded when Lincoln spoke, and he denied that they had a right to do so.
choiceExplanations: Seven states had already seceded when Lincoln spoke, and he denied that they had a right to do so.
Lincoln was answering the secession then under way.
No such proposal was made.
The ruling concerned the territories.
questions.distinguisher: The abolitionists choice is close because some followers of William Lloyd Garrison called for disunion, but Lincoln was answering the secession of the Southern states.
